clue.text: Pet hit (lorry doing for it)? Very emotionally involving

parts.note: a cat is a common household pet

indicators.note: one thing doing for another stands in for it, so the lorry replaces the word it in the clue

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
an artic is an articulated lorry, a big truck in British usage

explanation.surface: A puzzled aside about a pet being run over, followed by a remark on how moving it all is.
explanation.walkthrough: The lorry, ARTIC, does for (replaces) IT in HIT, giving HARTIC after CAT. ARTIC is everyday British shorthand for an articulated lorry.
explanation.definitionFit: Something cathartic releases pent-up feeling, so it is intensely moving.

clue.text: They're often thrown by people who have gone to pot

definitions.text: They're often thrown by people who have gone to pot

parts.words: They're often thrown by people who have gone to pot
parts.note: potters throw clay on a wheel, so people who have taken up pottery throw these pieces

explanation.surface: A dig at people who have let themselves go, hurling things about.
explanation.definitionFit: Potters shape clay pieces on a wheel, an action called throwing, and the fired products are pottery.

clue.text: Gentle touch when making Spanish snack

parts.note: a tap is a light touch
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

explanation.surface: A light tap given while preparing a little Spanish dish.
explanation.definitionFit: These are small savoury dishes served in Spanish bars.

clue.text: Urgent request for help: complete deal with most of single pack

parts.note: all means whole or complete
a deal of cards gives out hands to the players

indicators.note: most of a word means all but its last letter is used

parts.note: single means one
a pack of cards is a deck

explanation.surface: Someone at a card table wanting to finish a deal using nearly a full pack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most of' drops the last letter of ONE, leaving ON. The card-game vocabulary (deal, pack) is the surface; the definition is the naval call for everyone to help.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's call for every crew member to come up and help, used generally for any urgent appeal.

clue.text: Drunk getting out of working this evening

indicators.note: read as 'outside of', the word for drunk sits round the word for working

parts.note: tight is slang for drunk
on means working or operating

explanation.surface: A drunk is no longer fit for work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of' is read as 'outside of', a container signal, though the surface makes it look like 'no longer'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means during the present evening or night, a straight synonym.

clue.text: Company curtailed attempts to seize English group

indicators.note: the trimmed word for attempts grabs and holds the E within it
curtailed means cut short, so the last letter of the word goes

parts.note: tries are attempts

explanation.surface: A firm cuts back its efforts to take over an English group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'curtailed' cuts the last letter (an S) from the attempts word, and 'to seize' puts E inside what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: A coterie is a small exclusive circle of people, a kind of set or clique.

clue.text: Pale and poor quality? Not half true!

indicators.note: not here means without, so the half word is taken away

parts.note: trashy means of poor quality

indicators.note: half of the four-letter word is its first two letters

explanation.surface: Someone protests that a claim about pallor and shoddiness is only half right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half' of TRUE gives TR, and 'Not' removes it from TRASHY. The exclamation 'Not half true!' looks like a comment on the claim.
explanation.definitionFit: Ash is pale grey, so an ashen or ashy face is pallid.

clue.text: Copywriter possibly wrecked sole range

indicators.note: wrecked letters are broken up and put together in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A copywriter has ruined a single cooker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrecked' rearranges SOLERANGE. 'possibly' marks a copywriter as one example of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A coiner of catchphrases for advertising; a copywriter is one kind.

clue.text: Unthinking supporters urge accepting some, nothing less

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so the word for urge holds the other piece

parts.note: a yen is an urge or longing

indicators.note: less means minus, so the letter for nothing is removed

parts.note: taken as written
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Uncritical followers press for a little more, minus anything at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'less' takes O (nothing) out of SOME, leaving SME, which YEN is 'accepting', giving Y-SME-EN.
explanation.definitionFit: People who agree with whatever their leader says are sycophants who back without thought.

clue.text: Set new standards in the disposal of shellac?

definitions.meaning: to exceed the best previous performance
old 78 rpm discs were made of shellac, so smashing one gets rid of it

explanation.surface: Getting rid of an old shellac disc as a way to raise the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: Old gramophone records were pressed in brittle shellac, so breaking one disposes of shellac.
explanation.definitionFit: Beating the previous best in a sport is setting a new standard; physically smashing a 78 disc is the literal sense.

clue.text: Put back Prince occupying centre part of film

indicators.note: the letter for prince takes up the middle position of the word for part of a film

parts.note: a reel is one spool of a film

explanation.surface: A royal is put back into the middle section of a movie.
explanation.walkthrough: P goes into the very centre of REEL, between the two Es.
explanation.definitionFit: To repel attackers is to drive them back.

clue.text: Infamous criminal out soon, taking control of US state

indicators.note: the anagram seizes and holds the state's abbreviation inside it
criminal suggests something wrong, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: RI is the abbreviation for Rhode Island

explanation.surface: A notorious crook about to be freed takes over an American state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminal' rearranges OUTSOON as NOTO OUS, which is 'taking control of' RI (Rhode Island).
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone widely known for something bad.

clue.text: Fool bringing chap in for rodeo horse

indicators.note: with 'in', bringing a man in places him inside the word for fool
with 'bringing', in shows one word goes inside the other

parts.note: a mug is a gullible fool
Stan is a man's name, standing for any chap

explanation.surface: A fool brings a man along to ride at a rodeo.
explanation.walkthrough: The container signal is split: 'bringing' and 'in' sit either side of 'chap'.
explanation.definitionFit: A wild horse of the American plains, the kind ridden in rodeos.

clue.text: Bird goes round everyone carrying a good drop of beer?

indicators.note: the bird's name encloses the rest of the letters

parts.note: ree is a dictionary name for the female ruff, also called a reeve

indicators.note: carrying means holding, so the word for everyone holds the letter a

parts.note: all means everyone

explanation.surface: A bird circles a crowd that is clutching a nice pint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carrying' puts A inside the word for everyone, and the bird 'goes round' the result. REAL ALE is British cask-conditioned beer; ree is an old name for a female ruff.
explanation.definitionFit: Cask beer, conditioned in the barrel, prized by British drinkers as the proper stuff.

clue.text: Dramatic spectacle petered out with chap dropping piano clumsily

indicators.note: clumsily handled letters end up in a jumbled new order
dropping means losing, so the letter for piano leaves the word

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning softly

explanation.surface: A theatrical event fizzles when a man fumbles at the piano.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropping' removes P from CHAP to leave CHA; 'clumsily' rearranges PETEREDOUT plus CHA. 'out' looks like an anagram signal but is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A French phrase for a sudden sensational turn of events, especially on stage.

clue.text: Unexpectedly our man is right, identifying constellation

indicators.note: unexpectedly suggests things turning out differently, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: An astronomer is surprised that a colleague named a star group correctly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unexpectedly' is the anagram signal; 'identifying' is a link joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Little Bear, the group of stars containing Polaris.

clue.text: Charles sure gallops in huntsman style

indicators.note: a galloping word is thrown about, its letters jolted into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Charles is certain to ride at a gallop like a hunter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gallops' is the anagram signal on 'sure'. The answer is the French cookery term, as in chicken chasseur.
explanation.definitionFit: French for hunter; in cookery it names a dish in the hunter's style, with mushrooms and wine.

clue.text: Reason PCs had to work with little time for police procedure

indicators.note: put to work, the letters are set into a fresh order

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A reason why constables had to work briefly on a police task.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to work' rearranges REASONPCSHAD with T (little time). The police vocabulary is all surface.
explanation.definitionFit: British police power to halt a person and frisk them for weapons or drugs.

clue.text: Important front-rank Conservative is old-fashioned

parts.note: arch means chief or principal, as in arch-enemy
A1 means first-class; the 1 is read as the letter I

explanation.surface: A senior Tory politician is dismissed as behind the times.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 (first-rate) is written AI in crosswords, the digit 1 standing for the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Archaic means belonging to an earlier era, out of date.

clue.text: French writer produced rubbish about English

parts.note: did means produced, as in 'did a drawing'
rot means nonsense, rubbish

explanation.surface: A French author wrote nonsense on the subject of England.
explanation.walkthrough: Here 'about' means 'concerning', a link between the pieces, not a container signal: the three pieces run in clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: Denis Diderot was the eighteenth-century French philosopher who edited the Encyclopedie.

clue.text: Unidirectional, old to new? Certainly

parts.note: taken as written
ay is a form of aye, yes

explanation.surface: A question about whether change goes only from old to new, answered yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' links O and NEW; AY, a spelling of aye, means yes.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving or allowed in a single direction only, like a street with traffic going one way.

clue.text: Expression of refusal mostly limiting mother's travelling

indicators.note: limiting means enclosing, so the shortened phrase surrounds the word for mother
mostly means all but the last letter

parts.note: 'no dice' is a slang way to refuse
ma is mother; the 's is a link

explanation.surface: Saying no nearly always restricts a mother's movements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' drops the E of NO DICE, leaving NODIC, which is 'limiting' MA.
explanation.definitionFit: Nomadic people wander from place to place rather than settling.

clue.text: Doctor moves slowly, makes deep incision in channel

parts.note: edges means inches along

explanation.surface: A surgeon creeps forward and cuts deep into a canal.
explanation.walkthrough: The medical surface makes 'incision' look surgical; the definition is digging out a waterway bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Dredging scoops silt from the bed of a river or harbour to make it deeper.

clue.text: Heads for glamorous lady eclipsing front of hotel's showiness

indicators.note: eclipsing means blotting out, so the new letters cover the hotel name's opening letter

parts.note: the Ritz is a famous luxury hotel; the 's is a link

indicators.note: heads are the first letters of the following words

explanation.surface: Leading glamorous women outshine a grand hotel's showy display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heads for' takes G and L, which are 'eclipsing front of' RITZ, replacing its R to give GLITZ. The Ritz is a famous luxury hotel in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Glitz is flashy glamour, ostentatious display.

clue.text: Where one sits victory medal -fur?

parts.note: a win is a victory
GC stands for the George Cross, a British gallantry medal
fur is animal hair

explanation.surface: A clipped question about a winner's seat, medal and fur.
explanation.walkthrough: GC is the George Cross, Britain's highest civilian award for bravery.
explanation.definitionFit: A high-backed armchair with side pieces is a seat.

clue.text: Fruit's round, as it happens

parts.note: O is round in shape
live describes broadcasting at the moment it happens

explanation.surface: A fruit is round, as luck would have it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as it happens' sounds like 'by chance' but means broadcast in real time.
explanation.definitionFit: A small oval stone fruit grown for eating and oil.

clue.text: Retracted negative statement about king in story

indicators.note: about means around, so the reversed word surrounds the letter for king
retracted means drawn back, so the word for no is read in the other direction

parts.note: nay is an old word for no
R stands for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A withdrawn denial concerning a monarch features in a tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retracted' turns NAY into YAN, which goes 'about' R.
explanation.definitionFit: A yarn is a long tale, often far-fetched.

clue.text: Crazed tour endlessly going round French resort area

indicators.note: going round suggests letters spinning into a new order
endlessly means without its last letter

explanation.surface: A frenzied trip circling a French holiday coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' cuts the R from the trip word; 'going round' is the anagram signal. 'Crazed' looks like the signal but is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The French Riviera, the Mediterranean coast with resorts like Nice and Cannes.
